rw.headline: IER and MUA partner on engineering insurance
rw.dek: The Institute of Engineers Rwanda and MUA Insurance will offer tailored products and training to over 5,000 members.
paragraphs: The Institute of Engineers Rwanda (IER) and MUA Insurance signed a partnership agreement on Wednesday, October 28, at MUA's headquarters. This deal gives Rwanda's Engineering Practitioners access to specialized insurance products, reduced rates, and practical risk-management training. IER President Eng. Philbert Mbanza and MUA's Konde Bugingingo signed the accord, which covers engineers, technologists, technicians, and consulting firms.

Mbanza stated the partnership aims to secure cover suited to risks in design, construction, and on-site work, noting that a single insurer can offer better terms through pooled numbers. He also suggested the agreement could encourage more practitioners to join the IER, which has over 5,000 members and is growing by 25% annually. Professional indemnity insurance is among the products discussed, which Mbanza believes should be a necessity for practitioners.

Bugingingo explained that MUA will develop products for the distinct needs of engineering professionals, using risk data to improve safety and make their work easier. He added that pooling members could make insurance more affordable than individual purchases. MUA plans to tailor services for different roles, acknowledging varied risks. The collaboration also includes continuous professional development and aims to increase public confidence in infrastructure projects by ensuring risks are covered.

paragraphs: Rwanda’s Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva told a Russia–Africa youth forum in Moscow on October 29 that the country’s post-1994 Genocide recovery offers lessons on how young people can rebuild a nation.

Nsengiyumva stated that the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi killed over one million people in 100 days, and that the regime manipulated youth to fuel atrocities, while others fought to end the tragedy. He highlighted the Rwanda Patriotic Army’s choice of reconciliation over revenge after securing the country.

The Prime Minister urged young participants to use their skills for cross-border partnerships and noted Rwanda’s visa-free policy for African citizens as key for economic integration and shared prosperity.

rw.headline: Rwanda prime minister attends Russia-Africa summit
rw.dek: Dr Justin Nsengiyumva represented President Kagame at the Moscow gathering focused on expanding cooperation.
paragraphs: Rwanda's Prime Minister, Dr Justin Nsengiyumva, represented President Paul Kagame at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on October 28, 2026. The summit, which opened on October 28, aims to expand cooperation between Russia and African nations across various sectors. Nsengiyumva also spoke at the Russia-Africa Youth Forum at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) on October 28, sharing Rwanda’s development experience.

The summit agenda includes discussions on trade, investment, infrastructure, energy, agriculture, healthcare, and technology, with participants also set to explore cooperation in artificial intelligence and nuclear technology. The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed Nsengiyumva attended a reception hosted by Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 28. Rwanda and Russia established diplomatic relations in 1963.

This meeting is part of a series of Russia-Africa summits that began in 2019, with previous editions held in Sochi in 2019 and Saint Petersburg in July 2023. The 2023 summit produced cooperation documents including an action plan for 2023–2026 and agreements on counterterrorism and information security. Nsengiyumva arrived in Moscow on October 27, 2026, for the event.

rw.headline: Rwanda seeks $386 million from South Korean firm
rw.dek: The government filed a counterclaim at the Permanent Court of Arbitration over a failed 4G network project.
paragraphs: Rwanda has filed a $386 million counterclaim against South Korean telecommunications company KT Corporation over a failed 4G network project. The government, the Rwanda Development Board, the Rwanda Social Security Board, and the Agaciro Development Fund filed the claim on October 20, 2026, with the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

KT Corporation, which owns 51% of the joint venture KT Rwanda Networks (KTRN), disclosed the filing on October 23, stating it would challenge Rwanda's damage calculations. The dispute centres on the 2013 joint venture established to build and operate Rwanda’s 4G LTE broadband infrastructure.

The $386 million claim is equivalent to about Rwf 574 billion, more than 1.4 times Rwanda’s agriculture and livestock budget for 2026/27. It also represents about 7.3% of the nation's Rwf 7.796 trillion budget for the same fiscal year.

rw.headline: New Auditor General faces audit accountability gap
rw.dek: Claudette Mukashyaka urged to investigate why public institutions fail to implement audit recommendations.
paragraphs: Rwanda’s new Auditor General of State Finances, Claudette Mukashyaka, faces the challenge of improving the implementation of audit recommendations by public institutions. The Senate’s Committee on Economic Affairs and Finance raised this issue during her appointment review, also calling for annual audits of all entities receiving public funds.

Senator Dr Frank Habineza stated that Mukashyaka possesses the necessary academic and professional qualifications for the role, having worked at the Office of the Auditor General for four years. He noted her intention to enhance audit quality and meet international standards, but stressed the importance of institutions acting on audit findings. The latest annual report indicated that 65 per cent of audit recommendations were implemented in 2025, an increase from 60 per cent in 2024, covering 96 per cent of government expenditure across 252 public entities.

The report also showed improvements in financial management, with 97 per cent of public entities receiving unqualified audit opinions in 2025, up from 94 per cent in 2024. Compliance with laws and regulations saw an increase from 75 per cent to 83 per cent. Mukashyaka was appointed by the Cabinet on October 26, 2026, succeeding Alexis Kamuhire. Gratien Kubwimana was approved as Deputy Auditor General.

st.headline: Sao Tome and Principe bans plastic bags
st.dek: Law 8/2020 prohibits plastic bag production, import, and sale, with government to create incentives for alternatives.
paragraphs: Sao Tome and Principe banned plastic bags on September 21, 2020, through Law 8/2020. The law, published in the Official Gazette, prohibits the production, import, commercialization, and free distribution of plastic bags.

The legislation aims to curb plastic waste, following similar actions in Cabo Verde and Angola. The government is tasked with creating economic and administrative incentives to encourage private investment in alternative products.

Future revisions of the law could progressively ban other single-use plastic items like cups and cutlery, mirroring Cabo Verde's broader approach. The quality of alternative products must also be verified as per the law's implementation monitoring clause.

st.headline: Sao Tome and Principe to get first neurosurgeon in 3 years
st.dek: Elyane Neto, 26, returns to Russia for advanced training in a specialty currently unavailable in the nation.
paragraphs: Sao Tome and Principe's health system will gain its first neurosurgery specialist within three years. Elyane Neto, a 26-year-old doctor trained in Russia, will depart on Thursday for Moscow to pursue this specialization. Neto completed seven years of general medicine training at Moscow University and recently volunteered for two months at the Ayres de Menezes Central Hospital.

Neto stated that neurosurgery is a specialty that the country lacks, noting that many patients do not receive adequate care. She cited an increase in young people with neurological issues like strokes and head trauma from motorcycle accidents as reasons for the demand. Neto comes from a family of medical professionals, including her father, brother, aunt, and sister-in-law.

During two weeks in October, Neto collaborated with a team of eight Russian specialists who provided support in various surgical fields at the Ayres de Menezes Central Hospital. This group operated on dozens of Sao Tomean patients, highlighting a gap in local specialized surgical capacity.

st.headline: Príncipe residents face rising crime wave
st.dek: Assaults on homes and businesses are causing concern on the island, with residents reporting stolen goods.
paragraphs: Residents of Príncipe island are experiencing a growing wave of robberies targeting homes and businesses, creating unusual insecurity. Domingas da Conceição reported the loss of phone credit, cash, a mobile phone, and school bags. Arzemiro Cassandra also had his wallet stolen, along with a bag of potatoes from a storage area.

The fear of crime is widespread among traders and residents, who note a change from the island's historically safe past. Merchant António Barros recalled a time when valuables could be left unattended, contrasting it with the present situation. Residents suggest that nighttime power cuts, due to energy shortages, are enabling criminals by leaving areas in darkness.

Arzemiro Cassandra also stated that the island is becoming a refuge for individuals fleeing crimes committed in São Tomé. Security forces are being called upon to increase patrols and provide a more effective response to the escalating situation.

st.headline: Sao Tome and Principe, Angola sign higher education quality deal
st.dek: The agreement between ANRES and INAAREES will allow for the exchange of external evaluators and accreditation procedures.
paragraphs: Sao Tome and Principe's National Agency for Higher Education Regulation (ANRES) and Angola's National Institute for Evaluation, Accreditation and Recognition of Higher Education (INAAREES) signed a cooperation protocol in Luanda on October 29, 2026. The agreement aims to strengthen the quality assurance systems for higher education in both nations. ANRES President Sónia dos Reis Magalhães and INAAREES Director-General Jesus António Tomé signed the protocol.

This partnership will facilitate the exchange of external evaluators and the sharing of accreditation procedures between the two countries. It also covers the harmonization of academic equivalence processes and technical capacity building. A bilateral technical committee with up to six members will be formed to develop biannual action plans and monitor goals, meeting annually in Luanda and Sao Tome.

The protocol takes immediate effect and will last for an initial five-year period, with options for renewal. This accord is designed to align academic excellence policies within the Portuguese-speaking Community (CPLP).

sn.headline: Senegal doctors see stroke patients after eight-year waits
sn.dek: Saint-Louis health centre offered free consultations for stroke victims on October 29, 2026.
paragraphs: Saint-Louis residents struggling with stroke after-effects received free medical consultations on October 29, 2026, at the Ousmane Ngom health centre. The event, organised by the Senegalese Association for Support to Stroke Patients and Families (ASP-AVC), aimed to address the region's shortage of neurologists. Many patients had not seen a specialist for up to eight years.

Dr. Mame Maimouna Diaw Santos, a neurologist at the Saint-Louis regional hospital, saw about 40 patients during the event. She noted that stroke victims represent four out of every 10 neurology patients she sees. Dr. Diaw Santos stated she has been the sole neurologist at the facility since June 2021, highlighting the need for more specialists to manage patient care.

The free consultations also included screenings for high blood pressure and diabetes, along with medication donations. Community health workers, known as Badianou Gokh, also participated, emphasizing the need for ongoing awareness campaigns beyond the annual World Stroke Day. Dr. Diaw Santos stressed that prevention, including regular physical activity and managing conditions like hypertension and diabetes, is important.

sn.headline: Senegal releases 30 detained at MFDC Casamance headquarters
sn.dek: Authorities freed 30 individuals arrested during the Tuesday dismantling of the MFDC political wing's base in Ziguinchor.
paragraphs: 30 people arrested during the Tuesday dismantling of the political wing's headquarters of the Movement of the Forces of Casamance (MFDC) in Ziguinchor, southern Senegal, have been released. The security source confirmed the releases on Thursday to AFP. The headquarters, located on the outskirts of Ziguinchor, was the base for the MFDC's independence struggle in Casamance, which began in December 1982.

Gendarmes dismantled the site on Tuesday and detained 30 occupants, according to a security source. The last detainees were freed on Wednesday following instructions from the Ziguinchor public prosecutor. A source close to the MFDC stated that two individuals remained in custody, and reported 33 arrests on Tuesday. Local media also reported the seizure of MFDC flags and mobile phones.

Images showed gendarmes erasing MFDC inscriptions from walls and seizing documents, sound equipment, and chairs. A gendarmerie officer told local media that seized documents are being analyzed for useful information. The operation occurred on the anniversary of the October 27, 2019, death of rebel figure Abdou Elinkine Diatta.

sn.headline: Moody's downgrades Senegal's foreign currency debt rating
sn.dek: The rating agency lowered the long-term foreign currency debt rating from Caa2 to Ca, citing expected higher losses for external private creditors.
paragraphs: Senegal's public debt treatment plan, which excludes local currency debt, has led Moody's to downgrade the country's long-term foreign currency debt rating from Caa2 to Ca. The agency confirmed the local currency rating at Caa2 and short-term ratings at Not-Prime, while changing the outlook from negative to stable.

Moody's explained the foreign currency downgrade by anticipating external private creditors could face losses between 35% and 65% due to the debt treatment. The local currency debt was maintained at Caa2 because it will likely be excluded from the treatment but remains exposed to liquidity risks.
The stable outlook is partly attributed to Senegal's membership in the UEMOA, which helps limit financial risks and allows continued borrowing on the regional market.

sn.headline: Refugee athlete to compete at Dakar Youth Games
sn.dek: Arno Yafunga Botay will represent the Refugee Olympic Team in judo at the 2026 games.
paragraphs: Arno Yafunga Botay, a 15-year-old judoka, will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games. He qualified for the under-55kg category after trials in East Africa. This marks the first time a refugee team will participate in the Youth Games.

Botay, who fled the Democratic Republic of Congo with his family at age six, was surprised by his selection. "I didn't expect to be selected," he told BBC Sport Africa, adding, "I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy." His father, Arnold, also practised judo and taught him the sport.

Botay stated that representing other refugees and his community at the games means a great deal to him. His family settled in Nairobi after living in the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya, following threats to his father's life and an attack on their home.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone president warns kush sellers to stop
sl.dek: President Bio visits a drug rehabilitation facility and urges parents to find honest work.
paragraphs: President Julius Maada Bio has ordered sellers of the synthetic drug Kush to cease their illicit trade, which is causing widespread harm in Sierra Leone. During a visit to the Government’s Harmful Drug Rehabilitation Facility in Hastings on October 30, 2025, he assured recovering users of his administration’s commitment to stopping the sale of dangerous substances. He specifically implored parents involved in selling Kush to stop immediately and seek legitimate livelihoods.

The president addressed drug users at the rehab, stating that their future is essential for Sierra Leone’s development and that the government is working to break the drug supply chain. He condemned those producing and selling Kush, a drug linked to the deaths of many young people since 2019. Bio highlighted the establishment of rehabilitation centers in Hastings, Gondama, and Daru, with plans for another in Teko, Makeni.

Parents shared personal struggles, including Elizabeth Ansumana whose lawyer son became addicted to Kush and required government treatment. A former user, Margaret Jawara, now an ambassador against drug use, credited the Hastings facility and the Ministry of Social Welfare for her recovery. Minister of Social Welfare, Melrose Karminty, reported successful family reintegration for many victims. President Bio also launched a Presidential Task Force on Drugs and Substance Abuse.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burning causes deforestation
sl.dek: Burning wood for charcoal is destroying economic trees and leaving land exposed to climate change effects.
paragraphs: Charcoal burning, a common practice in Sierra Leone for cooking fuel, is leading to widespread deforestation and environmental degradation.  65-year-old Pa Alimamy, a charcoal burner for over two decades, stated his family relies on this trade for survival, highlighting its prevalence in Freetown and other towns due to limited access to electricity and clean cooking options. The National Energy Compact reports only 36% of the population has electricity and 15% clean cooking access.

The process of making charcoal involves cutting down trees, including valuable economic species like orange and mango, which exacerbates environmental hazards. Paul Lamin from the Environmental Protection Agency acknowledged the practice's negative impact, noting that the slow regrowth of trees reduces the land's capacity to absorb carbon. He also admitted that viable alternative energy sources are currently scarce for the population.

Experts warn that greenhouse gas emissions from charcoal production and use harm human health and the environment. A Food and Agricultural Organization report estimates traditional wood energy emits 2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, with Sub-Saharan Africa contributing a third of these emissions. Continued unsustainable charcoal practices are expected to worsen climate change, potentially reducing future wood-energy supplies.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone seeks Russian mining expertise
sl.dek: Minister Mattai wants Russian help with exploration, processing and training to boost mineral sector.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone is seeking Russian expertise to improve its mineral exploration and processing capabilities. Minister of Mines, Julius Daniel Mattai, spoke at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, calling for cooperation beyond raw material export. The country holds iron ore, diamonds, lithium, cobalt, nickel, and coltan.

Mattai stated that Sierra Leone needs better geological surveys, drilling, and modern geophysical investigations to understand its mineral deposits. He highlighted a June 2024 memorandum of understanding on mineral resource inventory for attracting investment. The minister also stressed the importance of local processing and manufacturing to create jobs and retain value, which requires infrastructure like electricity, roads, and ports.

The minister expressed interest in partnerships with Russian universities for scholarships, academic exchanges, and laboratory development in fields like geology and mining engineering. Cooperation on artificial intelligence for geological modelling and energy development to support industrial activities was also proposed.

sl.headline: Female artisanal miners report sexual violence in Kono district
sl.dek: Women working in the diamond-rich mines of Jaiama Nimikor face persistent threats of rape and harassment while scavenging for gold and diamonds.
paragraphs: Women working in the diamond-rich mines of Jaiama Nimikor in Sierra Leone's Kono district report frequent sexual violence while scavenging for minerals. Janet, a 32-year-old miner, recounted being raped at age 15 while working alone in the pits. She stated that she reported the assault to her village head at the time, but the perpetrator remained unidentified.

The violence has forced many women to flee their homes or face social stigma. Haja, a 48-year-old widow, said she was raped while working in the mines and subsequently fled to the village of Guitor. She reported the incident to a camp master, who dismissed her claim by suggesting the attacker was her partner. Haja stated that the man who assaulted her later left the village voluntarily.

Many women turned to artisanal mining as a primary source of income following the civil war. Janet, who dropped out of school as a teenager, continues to work in the sector to support her child. Other female miners in the area confirmed experiencing similar incidents of sexual harassment and assault while working in the pits.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone secures $60.97 million for immunisation
sl.dek: Gavi funding will expand malaria and hepatitis B vaccines through 2030.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone has secured US$60.97 million from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to boost childhood vaccinations until 2030. This funding under Gavi's 6.0 programme will support routine immunisation, including malaria vaccination and the hepatitis B birth-dose vaccine.

The Ministry of Health, led by Minister Dr Austin Demby, will use the funds to expand malaria vaccination to Western Area Urban, aiming to protect an additional 40,000 children annually. The hepatitis B vaccine will be given to infants within 24 hours of birth to prevent chronic infection.
The government has committed to meeting its co-financing obligations to sustain the programme. Sierra Leone has maintained routine vaccination coverage above 90% for the past five years.

so.headline: Somali army suffers heavy losses in Al-Shabaab ambush
so.dek: Hundreds of soldiers feared dead or wounded after militants attacked advancing forces near Burhakabo.
paragraphs: Somali army forces suffered significant casualties on Monday during an Al-Shabaab assault in the country's southwest. An estimated 2,000 troops advancing on Burhakabo were attacked in Jame’o village by militants using suicide car bombs. Al-Shabaab claimed to have killed 413 soldiers and wounded over 400, though these figures could not be independently verified.

The military's worst reverse in years saw troops fleeing within hours, with some remaining stranded in rural areas without a rescue operation, according to journalist Abdirizak Atosh. Military court chief Hassan Ali Nur Shute and ground forces commander Sahal Abdullahi Omar have opened an inquiry at Baledogle air base into the debacle. Commanders who abandoned the battlefield or military vehicles will face disciplinary action.

This rout is considered the army’s most severe defeat by insurgents since the 2023 Oswayne attack. Al-Shabaab also claimed that a Turkish air strike killed 15 captured special forces troops receiving medical treatment. Turkey reportedly destroyed some of its donated Kirpi armoured vehicles to prevent their propaganda use by militants, who claimed to have captured numerous army vehicles.

so.headline: AU troops to leave four bases in Somalia
so.dek: Peacekeepers will withdraw next week from Lower Shabelle region due to financial strain, impacting security near Mogadishu.
paragraphs: African Union peacekeepers will withdraw from four forward operating bases in Somalia’s Lower Shabelle region next week. The mission is scaling back under severe financial strain, according to local media reports on Thursday.

The pullback follows Washington's agreement to extend support for the mission until December 2027, after it threatened in July to cut logistical assistance. Analysts warn that Somali forces lack the capacity to occupy the sites quickly enough to prevent them from falling to Al-Shabaab militants.

Lower Shabelle is a strategic belt southwest of the capital, and AU deployments have helped shield Mogadishu. Somalia’s president Hassan Sheikh Mohamud travelled to Uganda this week urging President Yoweri Museveni to keep Ugandan troops in Somalia.

so.headline: African journalists adopt AI and decent work plan
so.dek: Leaders agreed an action plan for responsible AI, better working conditions, and quality journalism across Africa.
paragraphs: Journalist leaders from across Africa have agreed on an action plan to promote responsible artificial intelligence (AI), improve working conditions, and ensure quality journalism continent-wide. The plan was finalised in Addis Ababa on October 24-25, 2026, following a two-day dialogue organised by the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ). The programme brought together media leaders with representatives from the African Union Commission, UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), and the European Union (EU).

Participants discussed how AI impacts journalism, considering its potential for research and verification against risks like fabricated content and impersonation. They also addressed poor working conditions, including low pay, job insecurity, and pressure on editorial independence, exploring how AI automation might affect newsroom staffing. Safety and protection for journalists, including violence and digital harassment, were also key agenda items, with a focus on ending impunity for crimes against them.

The discussions were informed by FAJ's recent continental survey on journalists' conditions, which gathered responses from 1,586 journalists in 45 countries. This survey aims to provide a stronger evidence base for advocacy with media organisations and governments. The FAJ stated that artificial intelligence must not worsen the precarious conditions journalists already face.

ss.headline: Riek Machar praises late General Joseph Lagu
ss.dek: Machar, detained in a cell, called Lagu a selfless leader who prioritized peace and self-determination.
paragraphs: Former First Vice President Riek Machar on Wednesday described the late General Joseph Lagu as a leader who was not greedy for power. Machar, currently detained, conveyed his condolences in a message during the 125th session, praising Lagu's commitment to peace and self-determination for Southern Sudan.

Machar stated that Lagu deserved recognition for his contributions to the liberation struggle and for prioritizing the welfare of the people. He noted that Lagu left leadership to someone not originally part of the movement, highlighting his selfless nature. Lagu was a key figure in the Anyanya movement and helped negotiate the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement.

The Addis Ababa Agreement ended the first Sudanese civil war and granted Southern Sudan regional autonomy for a decade. Lagu, born in 1931 in Eastern Equatoria, became leader of the Southern Sudan Liberation Movement in 1968. He later served as president of the High Executive Council and Sudan's second vice-president before retiring from public service.

ss.headline: South Sudan secures $267 million for Ugandan electricity
ss.dek: The funding will extend power from Nimule to Juba and other major towns, aiming to boost reliability and affordability.
paragraphs: South Sudan's Ministry of Finance and Planning and the African Development Bank (AfDB) have agreed on $267 million to extend electricity from Uganda into the country. The project, launched on Wednesday, will bring power from Nimule to Juba and other major towns, improving supply reliability and affordability. This initiative aims to integrate South Sudan's power grid with Uganda's through a new interconnection.

Benjamin Ayali Koyongwa, the Finance Ministry's Undersecretary for Planning, thanked the AfDB and partners for their support during the launch. Fouzia Haji of the AfDB stated that electricity is vital for households and businesses and will support economic development in both nations. The launch was attended by officials from the Ministries of Energy and Dams, and Finance, along with Ugandan representatives.

The project follows the recent commissioning of electricity supply from Uganda to Nimule in Eastern Equatoria State. This extension is part of wider efforts to increase access to reliable electricity in South Sudan via regional power connections. The AfDB noted that electricity is essential for economic growth once the project is completed.

ss.headline: South Sudanese children demand climate action
ss.dek: Young participants in a Juba consultation called for climate-resilient schools and early warning systems.
paragraphs: Children in South Sudan have urged the government and world leaders to invest in practical measures against climate change impacts like flooding and drought. During a climate consultation in Juba on Thursday, young participants adopted a declaration demanding climate-resilient schools, accessible early warning systems, and emergency shelters. They described climate change as a child-rights crisis threatening education, food, water, and healthcare, especially for vulnerable communities.

Climate advocate Siama Santino, 17, shared how heat waves in 2024 and 2025 disrupted learning, and flooding in Bor made school travel difficult. The children's declaration stated that COP31 must deliver climate justice and action, not just promises. Some families in affected communities are reportedly eating only once a day due to crop failures and flooding.

The young participants also called for increased investment in climate education, safer schools, clean water access, and emergency services tailored to children's needs. They highlighted the heightened risks for children with disabilities, displaced children, and those in remote or conflict-affected areas. The demands come ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye.

ss.headline: South Sudan agrees to transfer Petronas oil shares to Russia
ss.dek: Zarubezhneft will take over stakes in DPOC and GPOC following Petronas' withdrawal.
paragraphs: South Sudan has agreed in principle to transfer former Malaysian oil company Petronas' shares in two oil consortiums to Russia's state-owned Zarubezhneft. The preliminary agreement was formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding and a Letter of Acceptance signed in Moscow on October 29. This move follows Petronas' official withdrawal from South Sudan's oil industry on August 7, 2024, after a previous sale attempt to Savannah Energy failed.

The shares are in the Dar Petroleum Operating Company (DPOC) and Greater Pioneer Operating Company (GPOC). South Sudan's Minister of Petroleum, Awow Daniel Chuang, and Russian Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilev were present at the signing. Nile Petroleum Corporation (NilePet) described Zarubezhneft as a suitable partner with experience in increasing production and improving infrastructure.

The transfer, discussed on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit, is expected to strengthen South Sudan's oil partnership with Russia. Zarubezhneft has over 50 years of international experience in developing oil and gas fields, particularly challenging ones. This agreement aims to create opportunities for greater economic cooperation and technical development in South Sudan's oil sector.

ss.headline: South Sudan to hold state funeral for General Joseph Lagu in Juba
ss.dek: The family of the late General Joseph Lagu Yanga has accepted President Salva Kiir's offer of a state funeral and burial in the capital.
paragraphs: The family of the late General Joseph Lagu Yanga has welcomed President Salva Kiir Mayardit's decision to grant him a state funeral, confirming his burial will be in Juba. Ambassador John Andruga, speaking for the family, stated that consultations with close relatives confirmed their agreement with the state funeral in Juba, as a village ceremony was not feasible. Andruga noted that Lagu was a national figure whose legacy belonged to all of South Sudan, not just his Madi community.

General Joseph Lagu Yanga died in Juba earlier this week at the age of 95. His death prompted tributes for his role in South Sudan’s liberation struggle, including leading the Anyanya One movement in 1963. Under his command, the movement gained momentum, leading to the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement that granted regional autonomy to Southern Sudan.

Lagu later served as president of the High Executive Council of the autonomous Southern Sudan region from 1978 to 1980 and as Sudan’s second vice president. He also represented Sudan at the United Nations in New York from 1990 to 1992. Lagu remained influential in South Sudan’s political history, supporting self-determination before the 2011 independence referendum.

sd.headline: Sudanese army drone strike kills 36 in Nyala market
sd.dek: Médecins Sans Frontières reported 150 wounded and widespread devastation after two strikes hit a busy market and a civilian neighborhood.
paragraphs: A Sudanese Armed Forces drone strike hit a busy market in Nyala, South Darfur State, on Monday, October 26, killing 36 people and injuring over 150. A second strike hit a civilian neighborhood in the city around 8 p.m. local time. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) stated that the Nyala Teaching Hospital, which it supports, received the bodies, with 21 victims identified as civilians.

MSF project coordinator Dale Koninckx described patients arriving at the hospital with shrapnel wounds and burns, transported from the market by tuk-tuks and donkey carts. "Medical staff worked around the clock treating patients, including women and children," Koninckx said, questioning why markets, essential for accessing food, are being targeted. He added that markets, homes, and civilian infrastructure are not legitimate targets and all conflict parties must protect civilians.

This attack follows a similar incident on October 16 in Nyala, where a drone strike on Al-Mawashi market killed at least four people. MSF noted that such incidents expose civilians to violence and limit access to food and supplies amid growing malnutrition concerns. The organization also reported that Rapid Support Forces carried out drone strikes on electricity infrastructure in other states recently.

sd.headline: UN, France condemn escalating drone attacks in Sudan
sd.dek: Drone strikes on civilian infrastructure are disrupting essential services and killing civilians, including children.
paragraphs: The United Nations and France have condemned escalating drone attacks across Sudan, warning that strikes on civilian infrastructure are disrupting essential services and killing civilians, including children. The French embassy in Sudan called the recent escalation of air strikes entirely unacceptable, citing attacks in Darfur, Khartoum, Abyei, the northern Nile Valley, Kordofan, and Blue Nile. These attacks have killed hundreds of civilians, including many children, within a few days.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) also expressed concern over continuing drone attacks, noting damage to vital civilian infrastructure and disruption of essential services for millions. A major electricity substation serving Khartoum state was struck on Tuesday, October 27, following strikes on power stations in El Gezira, Sennar, and El Gedaref states on Monday, October 26. Local authorities reported extensive damage, threatening the national electricity grid.

The UN’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan warned that expanding drone attacks and repression in El Obeid put civilians at increasing risk. Drone strikes attributed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) killed and injured civilians, damaged schools and displacement sites, and disrupted access to healthcare, electricity, and water in North Kordofan’s capital. The mission chair noted the conflict is becoming more geographically extensive, technologically sophisticated, and dangerous for civilians.

sd.headline: Sudan war displaces 27,400 families in Blue Nile
sd.dek: Intense fighting between the Sudanese army, RSF, and SPLA forces has driven thousands to seek shelter in overcrowded camps.
paragraphs: Fresh fighting between the Sudanese army, Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and the Sudan People’s Liberation Army (SPLA) has driven nearly 27,400 families from their homes in Sudan's Blue Nile state. Displaced people are fleeing into and across the state, adding to the strain on existing shelters. Many are escaping conflict in El Kurmuk, Geissan, and Wad El Mahi localities, while others are returning from South Sudan.

Humanitarian Aid Commissioner Qisma Abdel Karim Deldoum reported that Damazin locality alone hosts 12 camps, with El Karama (5) sheltering 4,814 families and the Agricultural Research Centre accommodating 3,913. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) stated in September that nearly 100,000 people had been displaced in Blue Nile between January and August, with children making up 47% of this number.

The number of internally displaced people in Blue Nile has risen by 21% since the August update, according to the IOM. Camps like Al-Karama 3 have not received food aid for four months, according to its manager.

sd.headline: China deploys anti-drone systems in Abyei after attack
sd.dek: Chinese peacekeepers reinforced UNISFA after a drone attack killed UN personnel in the disputed region.
paragraphs: Chinese peacekeepers deployed anti-drone detection and jamming equipment in the disputed Abyei region on October 28, following a drone attack on a market on October 19 that killed members of a United Nations peacekeeping force. China’s Ministry of National Defence stated the specialised equipment aims to detect and jam drones and strengthen security to prevent further attacks. A Chinese peacekeeping rapid-response force returned to its camp after completing a security reinforcement mission.

The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) requested the Chinese peacekeepers’ assistance to reinforce a Pakistani infantry battalion after the October 19 attack. Upon arrival, the Chinese force deployed anti-drone systems and strengthened defensive measures against potential aerial attacks. The security operation included using surveillance drones to monitor the market and secure the surrounding area.

UNISFA’s leadership praised the Chinese peacekeepers for their swift response and professionalism, stating their intervention helped protect lives and property and strengthen stability in the region. The reinforcement mission concluded after the security situation stabilised, allowing the Chinese force to return to its camp.

tg.headline: Burkina Faso reinstates death penalty for economic crimes
tg.dek: Togo's proximity raises questions about applying similar strictness to its own economic crimes.
paragraphs: Burkina Faso reinstated the death penalty on October 20, 2026, with 71 lawmakers unanimously adopting a new penal code. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated the code targets terrorism, espionage, and treason, alongside economic and financial crimes that lead to death.

The new law also imposes life imprisonment and triple fines for embezzling public funds, with significantly increased fines for all offenses. This move by the military leader Captain Ibrahim Traoré follows his intention announced in December 2025.

Human rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch condemned the law, fearing it could suppress dissent. The strictness of Burkina Faso's new code prompts questions in Togo, a neighbor, about how such laws would apply to its own history of unpunished economic crimes.

tg.headline: Togo lawyers debate regional court's power over constitution
tg.dek: Jurists gathered at the University of Lomé on October 29, 2026, to discuss human rights courts and state sovereignty.
paragraphs: Jurists from across the region met at the University of Lomé on October 29 and 30, 2026, to discuss the role of regional courts. The conference focused on how these courts interact with the rule of law, constitutional changes, and state sovereignty.

A key discussion point was the ECOWAS Court of Justice's January 29, 2026, ruling on Togo's March 2024 constitutional reform. Opposition parties and civil society groups brought the case, arguing the reform violated certain principles. The government contested the court's jurisdiction over internal constitutional matters.

The debate continues over the ruling's implications, with some opposition groups viewing it as a judicial validation of illegitimacy. However, the court did not order the repeal of the constitutional law or any financial reparations, and the government maintains the court lacks authority for such control.

tn.headline: Tunisia energy deficit hits 10.48 billion dinars
tn.dek: Foreign exchange reserves fell to cover 93 days of imports by October 23, 2026.
paragraphs: Tunisia's energy trade deficit reached 10.48 billion dinars, nearly half of the country's total trade deficit. Foreign exchange reserves dropped to cover 93 days of imports as of October 23, 2026, down from 107 days a year earlier. These figures were presented on October 29 by Finance Minister Mechkat Salma Khaldi during a budget execution hearing.

Imports grew by 13.1% while exports increased by 8.6%, widening the trade balance pressures and increasing external financing needs. The energy deficit alone accounted for approximately 50% of the overall trade deficit. The minister also noted potential impacts from the Middle East geopolitical crisis on trade and energy prices.

Despite these challenges, tourism revenue rose by 3.7% and remittances from Tunisians abroad increased by 4.4%, helping to finance part of the external deficit. The government is also developing a plan to integrate informal economic activities into the legal framework to broaden the formal economic base and improve tax compliance.

tn.dek: The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists and the Tunisian Association of Democratic Women met on October 29, 2026, to discuss press freedom.
paragraphs: The president of the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT), Zied Dabbar, met with a delegation from the Tunisian Association of Democratic Women (ATFD) on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The ATFD delegation, led by its president Raja Dahmani, congratulated the SNJT on its new executive bureau.

During the meeting, the ATFD reaffirmed its solidarity with journalists and its support for initiatives defending freedom of the press and expression. Both organizations agreed to strengthen their cooperation to protect fundamental rights and combat restrictions and prosecutions targeting media professionals, according to an SNJT statement.

The two groups also discussed the state of freedoms in Tunisia and the challenges facing the journalism profession. This meeting occurred on the same day the head of government, Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri, met with the Tunisian community in Russia to discuss their contributions to national development.

tn.headline: Tunisia braces for thunderstorms and scattered rain
tn.dek: The national weather service forecasts localized storms and scattered showers across the country on Friday, October 30, 2026.
paragraphs: Tunisia will experience cloudy skies on Friday, October 30, 2026, with a risk of localized thunderstorms in the morning and scattered rain, particularly along the coast. Maximum temperatures will range between 22 and 26 degrees Celsius depending on the region. The wind will blow from the northwest at a weak to moderate intensity across the territory, and the sea will be slightly to moderately rough along the coasts.

The Institute National de la Météorologie (INM) predicted scattered, temporarily stormy showers for Thursday, October 29, 2026, which could be locally abundant with hail in some areas. These rains were expected to spread from the North to the Center and South throughout the day. Maximum temperatures on Thursday were forecast between 20 and 25 degrees Celsius, reaching 27 degrees Celsius in the Southwest.

On Thursday, the wind was expected to blow from the northwest in the North and Center, and from the east in the South. It could strengthen temporarily during stormy episodes, especially in the far South. The sea was predicted to be slightly agitated.

tn.headline: Club Africain beats Bizertin 3-2 in Ligue 1
tn.dek: Espérance de Tunis drew 0-0 with Club Sportif Sfaxien, while Stade Tunisien won 1-0.
paragraphs: Club Africain secured a 3-2 victory over Club Athlétique Bizertin in a delayed Ligue 1 match on Thursday, October 29. This win allows Club Africain, who had nine points from four games, to improve their league position after their African Champions League qualification. The defeat ended Club Athlétique Bizertin's positive run, which included a 3-1 win against ES Hammam-Sousse.

In Sfax, Club Sportif Sfaxien and Espérance de Tunis played to a goalless draw. Espérance de Tunis, with 12 points from five matches before this game, and Club Sportif Sfaxien, with eight points, both failed to gain ground in the race for the top places. Stade Tunisien returned to winning ways with a 1-0 victory over Espérance de Zarzis.

Espérance de Tunis missed an opportunity to extend their lead with the draw, while Club Sportif Sfaxien also failed to gain ground. Stade Tunisien's win follows a previous loss to US Ben Guerdane and aids their league progression. These matches were part of the sixth round of Ligue 1.

tn.headline: Tunisia podcasts festival returns after three-year break
tn.dek: The Podcast Days event will feature creators from Algeria and Marseille, celebrating sound creation.
paragraphs: The Tunisia Podcasts Festival, known as Podcast Days, will take place in Tunis on Friday, November 6 and Saturday, November 7, 2026. The event will be held at the auditorium of the Institut français de Tunisie (IFT) and L’Art Rue (Dar Bach Hamba) in the medina. This festival celebrates sound creation through meetings, masterclasses, round tables, public recordings, and immersive experiences.

Entry to the festival is free upon registration, following a three-day event in December 2023 that gathered podcasters, listeners, and professionals. This year's event is more condensed, featuring an opening evening, a full day, and a closing evening. Guests from Algiers and Marseille are expected to attend.

Raouia Kheder, founder of the Tunisia Podcasts Festival, stated that Tunisian podcasts have grown significantly since 2023, finding their voices, audiences, and models. She added that the Podcast Days aim to provide a space for creators to meet, learn, and observe work from across the Mediterranean.

zm.headline: Zambian president directs halt to plot allocations without infrastructure
zm.dek: President Hichilema tasks Housing Minister Christopher Kalila to address the 1.5 million housing deficit and enforce planning standards.
paragraphs: President Hakainde Hichilema has ordered Housing Minister Christopher Kalila to stop local councils from allocating plots without basic infrastructure, aiming to curb unplanned settlements. The President also directed Transport and Logistics Minister Charles Milupi to speed up the movement of goods along economic corridors to boost investment and economic growth.

Speaking at a swearing-in ceremony, President Hichilema stressed the need for strengthened urban planning, stating that all housing land must include essential services like roads to prevent public health issues. He urged Minister Kalila to tackle Zambia's estimated 1.5 million housing deficit while ensuring local authorities adhere to proper planning requirements.

The President also called for more multi-storey buildings to maximize land use and for affordable housing initiatives supported by effective mortgage systems. Minister Milupi was tasked with ensuring road and railway infrastructure supports faster and safer transportation of goods, as economic corridors are vital drivers of development.

zm.headline: Court nullifies UPND Mapatizya seat
zm.dek: High Court Judge Kazimbe Chenda ruled the election of Emelda Munashabantu premature due to tallying irregularities.
paragraphs: The Lusaka High Court has nullified the election of UPND’s Emelda Munashabantu as Mapatizya member of parliament. High Court Judge Kazimbe Chenda delivered the ruling in Livingstone, stating the declaration of Munashabantu as winner was premature. The election results were based on data from 64 of the constituency’s 75 polling stations.

The court heard that Munashabantu had polled 14,812 votes before the full tally was complete. The nullification followed a successful election petition citing irregularities in the tallying and declaration process for the August 13, 2026 parliamentary elections. Mapatizya Constituency in Zimba District is now without a Member of Parliament.

Judge Chenda ruled that serious irregularities in the post-voting electoral process affected the outcome of the August 13, 2026 parliamentary election. The UPND party has lost its Mapatizya seat following this court decision.

zm.headline: Mandevu by-election candidate withdraws citing threats
zm.dek: Forum for Democracy and Development candidate Daniel Chisenga pulled out of the race for the Mandevu seat.
paragraphs: Forum for Democracy and Development (FDD) candidate Daniel Chisenga withdrew from the November 5 Mandevu by-election, citing threats to his life from unknown individuals and political players. His withdrawal leaves UPND candidate Adrian Banda as the sole contender for the seat, which has over 123,000 registered voters.

Mr Chisenga stated he has informed the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) of his decision. The remaining candidates for the Mandevu seat are Adrian Banda of the UPND, Ntazana Musukuma of the Leadership Movement, and independent Daniel Daka. The ECZ is training 730 poll staff in Lusaka to ensure professionalism and impartiality.

ECZ vice-chairperson Vincent Mukanda urged poll staff to uphold integrity and fairness during the by-election. Acting chief electoral officer Collins Kachaka also stressed the importance of accurate record-keeping and control at polling stations. The by-election is scheduled for next Thursday.

zm.headline: Zambia starts cholera vaccine plant construction next month
zm.dek: The facility at Lusaka South Multi Facility Economic Zone will produce 20 million doses annually.
paragraphs: Construction of Africa’s first oral cholera vaccine manufacturing plant will begin next month at the Lusaka South Multi Facility Economic Zone. President Hakainde Hichilema announced the project, which is a collaboration between Zambia and Chinese company International Medical Technology. The plant is expected to produce 20 million doses of the vaccine each year.

President Hichilema stated the plant demonstrates Zambia’s commitment to cholera prevention and continental efforts to eliminate the disease by 2030. He also announced that the government released K13 million for the emergency supply of safe water amid a cholera outbreak. This outbreak has reached 1,622 cases and 30 deaths since July 28, affecting 20 districts across six provinces.

As of October 28, 104 patients remained admitted to hospitals, with 1,488 having recovered. The Ministry of Health reported 74 new cases in the latest 24-hour period, with no new fatalities. Minister of Health Roma Chilengi urged prompt delivery of safe water to affected communities with proper accountability for the K13 million funding.

eh.headline: Polisario Front faces choices before UN vote
eh.dek: Tensions rise in Tindouf and Algiers over a new UN resolution framework for Western Sahara.
paragraphs: The Front Polisario faces decisions that could reshape its organization and leadership as the UN Security Council prepares to vote on a new resolution framework for Western Sahara. On October 26, 2026, five days before the vote, Sahrawi women and children demonstrated in the Tindouf camps against the American proposal. Media outlets linked to the Front Polisario circulated images of these protests, aiming to project an image of unity.

A recording attributed to Bachir Mustapha emerged the following day, adding to internal discussions. These reactions, observed in both Tindouf and Algiers, highlight emerging tensions and strategies that could alter the future of the Polisario Front.

The proposed UN resolution framework has placed the Front Polisario at a crossroads. The reactions from within the camps and from Algerian officials indicate a complex internal dynamic as the organization confronts this moment.

eh.headline: US revises Western Sahara resolution draft
eh.dek: Draft changes autonomy from 'only viable' to 'most viable' solution, adding self-determination conditions.
paragraphs: The United States has revised a draft UN Security Council resolution on Western Sahara, changing the description of Moroccan autonomy from the "only viable solution" to the "most viable solution." This adjustment, detailed in an October 24 document, also reintroduces conditions for a just and mutually acceptable political solution, including respect for the UN Charter and the principle of self-determination.

The Polisario Front explained these changes on October 26, noting that while Moroccan autonomy remains the sole basis for negotiation, the revised text softens previous expectations. The shift away from presenting autonomy as the exclusive option aims to reduce interpretations of a historical turn favoring Morocco.

The revised draft also modifies the mission's name, proposing a change to MINUSO, and abandons the automatic transformation of MINURSO. These amendments emerged from consultations with other Security Council members, leading to a "war of drafts" focused on autonomy, self-determination guarantees, and the mission's future.

eh.headline: Lavrov and Attaf discuss Western Sahara in Moscow
eh.dek: Russian and Algerian foreign ministers met amid UN Security Council talks on a US draft resolution.
paragraphs: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed the Western Sahara issue with his Algerian counterpart Ahmed Attaf in Moscow on October 27, 2026. The ministers also reviewed bilateral relations and regional matters during their meeting on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.

The talks occurred as the UN Security Council held intensive consultations on a US draft resolution concerning Western Sahara and the MINURSO mandate. Lavrov expressed satisfaction with the trade, economic, and military-technical cooperation between Russia and Algeria.

Russia, a permanent Security Council member with veto power, maintains its traditional stance favoring a political solution within the UN framework, emphasizing self-determination. Moscow has abstained from voting on Western Sahara resolutions since 2018, citing concerns over the US-led drafting process.

ls.headline: Lesotho to chair SADC security organ
ls.dek: Prime Minister Sam Matekane's election follows a decade of regional scrutiny for instability.
paragraphs: Lesotho will chair the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation starting in 2026. Prime Minister Sam Matekane was elected to the position at an extraordinary SADC summit, marking a significant diplomatic achievement for the nation.

This appointment signifies a turnaround in Lesotho's regional standing after years of observation due to political instability and security-sector failures. The country was placed under the Organ’s agenda in 2014 following an attempted military coup and subsequent political troubles, including assassinations and troop deployments.

Foreign Affairs Minister Limpho Tau described the appointment as an honour for all Basotho, emphasizing it is a national responsibility. The role requires continued reform and accountability at home to credibly address regional security challenges.

ls.headline: Mafeteng Hospital sued for M2 million over alleged negligence
ls.dek: A patient claims he received no medical attention for seven days after a stomach operation in December 2024.
paragraphs: Mafeteng Hospital faces a M2 million lawsuit for alleged medical negligence after a patient claimed a botched surgery left faecal matter leaking into his body. Teboho Rammusi alleges he received no medical attention for seven days following surgery for a stab wound in December 2024 before being transferred to Tšepong Hospital and later Bloemfontein, South Africa. He is suing the Ministry of Health, its Principal Secretary Matšoanelo Monyobi, Minister Mamokete Ntšekhe, the hospital's Medical Superintendent, and the Attorney General.

In court papers, Rammusi accuses Mafeteng Hospital of failing to provide adequate care and qualified practitioners, stating that tubes on his body showed faeces leaking. Doctors at Tšepong Hospital reportedly discovered faecal matter had spilled into his abdominal cavity through punctured intestines. Rammusi claims this negligence resulted in additional medical expenses, a severe lung infection, pain, and suffering.

The lawsuit alleges the hospital's medical superintendent agreed to perform surgery with reasonable professional skill and care but failed to ensure suitably qualified practitioners were available. Rammusi claims the government is liable as Mafeteng Hospital is state-owned and its officers were acting within their employment scope.

ls.headline: Lebona Lephema considers new party after RFP leadership bid fails
ls.dek: Business tycoon Lebona Lephema may form a new political party if his attempt to unseat Nthomeng Majara as RFP deputy leader fails.
paragraphs: Disgruntled business tycoon Lebona Lephema is considering forming a new political party and leaving the Revolution for Prosperity (RFP). Lephema, a founding member of the RFP, believes he is entitled to the deputy leadership position currently held by Nthomeng Majara.

Lephema fell out with Prime Minister Sam Matekane after resisting a ministry split and his subsequent redeployment. He was dismissed from Cabinet in May after refusing to accept a new portfolio, citing potential conflicts of interest with the Lesotho National Development Corporation.

If his bid to wrestle the RFP deputy leadership from Majara fails, Lephema plans to form his own party. He has reportedly consulted with disgruntled members of the All Basotho Convention (ABC), including former minister Chalane Phori and ex-secretary-general Lebohang Hlaele, though both deny the claims.

ls.headline: Likuena coach warns of player fitness slump
ls.dek: Bob Mafoso reports aerobic fitness has dropped significantly ahead of November AFCON qualifiers.
paragraphs: Lesotho's national football team, Likuena, is facing a significant drop in player fitness, according to coach Bob Mafoso. Locally based players reported for a non-residential training camp on Monday, where physical assessments revealed a decline in aerobic capacity and endurance. The team is preparing for back-to-back 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers against Gabon next month.

Mafoso stated that approximately 80 percent of players who previously completed the Bronco Test in four minutes and 28 seconds are now taking four minutes and 52 seconds. He also expressed concern over players' strength levels, noting that physical conditioning requires urgent attention. Despite the findings, Mafoso insisted the technical team has three weeks to improve player condition before the crucial matches.

Likuena lost their opening two AFCON qualifiers to Niger and Morocco, and positive results against Gabon are needed to revive qualification hopes. The team will face Gabon's Panthers in Libreville on November 13 and in Polokwane, South Africa, on November 17. Mafoso stressed that player pressure should be reflected in preparation, not just on match day.
